answers.answer: I do NOT ship this A3 cable render toward sampling as-is; I decompose it against the three Flux traps FIRST. Trap 1 impossible knits: the 'deep interlocking rope cables' risk being non-stitch-conserving cables (Flux renders cable crossings that do not conserve wales), the 'wale-shifting rib transition' is a wale-changing rib (Flux renders width changes a real needle bed cannot execute), and the 'seamless-reading collar seam' is likely an un-linkable seam as drawn - all three are exactly what Flux renders WRONG and a human must catch before money moves. Who catches each: the T3 CAD/flat-knit programmer authoring the needle-action program catches non-stitch-conserving cables and wale-changing ribs (must re-author to conserve wales / stage the rib legally); linking/construction feasibility of the collar is confirmed by the programmer + a physical PPS swatch; I (design) catch them at the image-to-producible review before hand-off. Trap 2 un-payable colourwork: N/A here if A3 stays single-colour body per the budget (a cable A3 should be texture-led, not 6-colour). Trap 3 pill-risk: lower for merino/lambswool than acrylic, but any brushed surface still checks against the post-wash grade. Does 'fashioning marks as a premium FF cue' survive the linker-throughput constraint? Fashioning marks + cable + fine links-links are PRICED into A3 precisely because A3 is the premium halo that can pay for extra yarn and linker time - but the SAME render's deep cables and collar also DEMAND linker/knit time, so 'fashioning marks as a cue' survives ONLY if the total construction stays inside what the A3 tier can pay for; if the render piles cable + wale-shift + heavy fashioning + un-linkable collar, it exceeds the linker throughput the tier funds and I hold/redesign. Shipping the render as a spec without a programmer-authored program + a passing PPS swatch burns a ~2-5 wk sampling cycle plus dye-lot money [ESTIMATE], so the verdict is HOLD-for-programmer-and-swatch, not ship.
